findings.title: Local cache is populated before the DB write, so rejected devices bypass the limit on retry
findings.body: In tagDeviceUI, the local cache entry for the device is set (a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})) BEFORE calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, which now propagates up to Anonymous.Authenticate and rejects the request. However, the device's cache key has already been written, so for the next 29 minutes every subsequent request from that same device hits the cache and returns nil without ever touching the database — meaning authentication succeeds. The net effect is that a device over the limit is blocked exactly once and then freely allowed in on any retry, which defeats the feature. The cache entry should only be set after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds.

findings.title: Device limit check is racy: COUNT then INSERT is not atomic
findings.body: CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by first running CountDevices and only inserting if count < deviceLimit, with no transaction or database-level constraint tying the two together. Two concurrent requests for distinct new devices can both observe count < limit and both insert, exceeding the configured limit. With multiple Grafana replicas each doing this independently (and per-instance local caches), the overshoot can be larger. If the limit is meant to be enforced (e.g., for licensing/abuse control), the check-and-insert needs to be atomic (single transaction with locking, or a conditional INSERT based on a subquery count).

findings.title: Device-limit rejection surfaces as a raw error, producing HTTP 500 for end users
findings.body: When TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, Authenticate now returns that plain error (return nil, err). The authn layer has no typed handling for this error, so anonymous users who exceed the device limit will get a generic HTTP 500 Internal Server Error with the message 'device limit reached' instead of a deliberate status such as 429 Too Many Requests (or 401) with a user-facing explanation. The error should be wrapped in a typed authn/response error that maps to an appropriate status code and message.

findings.title: Device tagging moved onto the synchronous auth path without timeout or panic recovery
findings.body: Previously TagDevice was invoked in a background goroutine guarded by recover() and a 2-minute timeout (timeoutTag), so a slow or panicking database call could not affect request authentication. This PR calls a.anonDeviceService.TagDevice synchronously inside Authenticate with no timeout and no panic guard. On every local-cache miss (at least once per ~29 minutes per device per instance) the anonymous authentication path now blocks on a COUNT plus an UPDATE/INSERT against the database, and any panic in that path will crash the request. Consider keeping the failure isolation (timeout/recover) while still propagating the limit error.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined infers property type 'undefined'
findings.body: In GrafanaBootConfig, the new field is declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;`. Under strictNullChecks this gives the class property the literal type `undefined`, so any TypeScript consumer reading config.anonymousDeviceLimit sees type `undefined` and cannot use it as a number without a cast. The neighboring fields use explicit annotations (e.g. `loginError: string | undefined = undefined;`). This should be `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;` to match the GrafanaConfig interface. Note also that the Go DTO (FrontendSettingsDTO.AnonymousDeviceLimit, an int64 without omitempty) always serializes a number, so the value is never actually undefined in boot data.

findings.title: New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample config or docs
findings.body: The PR adds a new configuration key `device_limit` under [auth.anonymous] (read via anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)) but does not add it to conf/defaults.ini, conf/sample.ini, or the administration documentation, where all other auth.anonymous options (enabled, org_name, org_role, hide_version) are documented. Admins have no way to discover the setting, its default (0 = unlimited), or its semantics without reading the source.

findings.title: No test that an existing device can still update when the limit is reached
findings.body: TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only covers the rejection path (a brand-new device being refused with ErrDeviceLimitReached when the limit is reached). There is no test for the complementary updateDevice success path: an already-registered device that is at/over the limit must still be able to refresh its row (client_ip/user_agent/updated_at), otherwise legitimate returning devices would be locked out. There is also no test covering the interaction with the service-level local cache (i.e., that a rejected device is not cached and is re-checked on retry).
